analysis.one_liner: Makes tacit price coordination among competitors illegal price fixing under antitrust law.
analysis.headline: The Competitive Prices Act, which would make tacit price coordination among competitors a form of illegal price fixing, died in House committee without a markup or a vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal antitrust law so that when big companies in the same market quietly match each other's price moves without a written deal — what economists call 'conscious parallelism' — that conduct could be treated as illegal price fixing in civil lawsuits. Courts have long thrown out such cases unless plaintiffs can prove the companies acted together rather than independently; the bill would lower that bar, set out how plaintiffs can win such cases, and let companies respond with evidence that their pricing was independently rational. It applies to lawsuits by consumers, businesses, states, the federal government, and the FTC, but not to criminal prosecutions.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and small businesses that buy from industries where a few large firms set similar prices — such as airlines, fuel, food, and insurance — because companies that quietly coordinate prices could be sued for triple damages under the Sherman Act, raising the cost of coordinated overcharging.

how_it_helps.text: Makes 'consciously parallel pricing coordination' — a tacit agreement among two or more firms to raise, lower, change, maintain, or manipulate prices for interchangeable products or services — a prohibited form of price fixing under the Sherman Act in civil cases [S2] [S3].

Lets a plaintiff establish a case by showing that two or more companies took substantially similar pricing action at substantially the same time with substantially similar motivation, after which the burden shifts to the company to show its pricing was independently rational business judgment [S3].

Overturns court standards (including the Twombly pleading rule) that required plaintiffs to rule out the possibility of independent action, which the bill's findings say have blocked meritorious price-fixing cases from reaching trial [S3].
Applies to civil suits brought by consumers and businesses, state attorneys general, the United States, and the FTC, but does not change criminal price-fixing prosecutions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large companies in concentrated industries that rely on parallel pricing would face new lawsuit exposure and potential triple damages under the Sherman Act, and some of those costs could be passed to consumers if courts later found pricing was legitimate.

drawbacks.text: Economists have long argued that firms in concentrated markets often move prices in parallel because it is independently rational — matching a competitor's price is normal competitive behavior, not collusion — and the bill would expose that conduct to litigation, raising the risk of suits against legitimate pricing decisions [S3].

The bill shifts the burden of production to defendants after a fairly low threshold showing, which honest supporters would acknowledge invites more litigation cost for businesses even where no collusion exists [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: when a handful of firms dominate a market and quietly keep prices aligned, consumers have almost no way to sue under current law, and the bill would open that door. The cost is genuine uncertainty for firms whose pricing may be independently rational, and some cases would punish normal competitive matching. On balance the bill is a consumer-protection measure with a defensible evidentiary structure — it still requires plaintiffs to show similar motive and lets defendants rebut with rational business judgment — but its breadth means businesses would face meaningful new legal risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its antitrust subcommittee, but the committee never reported it and no vote ever took place before the Congress ended [S5] [S1].

narrative.text: Katie Porter introduced the bill on September 6, 2022, joined by four Democratic colleagues including Judiciary Committee Chairman Jerrold Nadler [S3] [S4].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction and to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law on November 1, 2022 [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large firms in concentrated industries that rely on parallel pricing avoided new civil antitrust liability, since the bill never advanced; consumers gained nothing because the cases it would have enabled were never created.

industries.industry: Large firms in concentrated markets (e.g., airlines, fuel, food processing, insurance)
industries.note: The bill would let consumers, businesses, states, and federal enforcers sue these firms for tacit price coordination with triple damages, a major new liability that current court-made pleading standards largely screen out [S3]. Their interest in killing the bill runs directly against consumers' interest in lower, competitively set prices.
Lawyers and firms bringing class-action antitrust cases would get a far easier path past motions to dismiss and summary judgment, since they would no longer need to rule out independent action [S3].
Defending companies against the expanded claims would generate new legal work, though this is a secondary effect of the bill's liability shift [S3].
